steps.title: Rhythm, intonation and questions
steps.body: Melody is part of meaning in French. Two simple rules cover most of what you need.

steps.title: Melody
rows: Question with a question word (où, quand, comment...)
rises on each item, falls on the last
Du pain ↗, du lait ↗, des pommes ↘.

steps.title: Rhythm, intonation and questions
steps.body: Rhythm. Cut the sentence into small groups. Each syllable has the same length. The last syllable of each group is a little longer and higher. Je m'appelle Sam. = zhuh-mah-PELL-sam. Tu parles français ? = tü-pahrl-frah(n)-SEH ↗.

steps.title: In Canada
steps.body: In Québec, a yes/no question often ends with a small word -tu: Tu viens-tu ? (Are you coming?). It is informal speech. In the exam use Tu viens ? or Est-ce que tu viens ?.

steps.question: What did you hear?
steps.explain: Voice goes up: it is a yes/no question.

steps.question: What did you hear?
steps.explain: Voice goes down: it is a statement.

steps.question: What does the person want to know?
steps.explain: Où est la gare ? means Where is the station?

steps.title: Speaking: Melody practice
steps.body:
Say each sentence twice, once as a statement and once as a question: Il parle français. · Il parle français ? Record yourself and compare.

• Exaggerate the melody at first. Then make it smaller.

steps.fr: Il parle français. (↘) Il parle français ? (↗)
steps.en: Model answer. Say it in your own words after.
steps.tip: Listen, then say it out loud. Tap Ask Marie to have her listen to you.
